checkpoints: Problem 1 (scaling): the pipeline's `agent { label 'builder' }` always binds to the same single static VM with a fixed executor count, so 20 concurrent builds must queue with no way to add capacity except manually standing up another VM.

Problem 2 (security): building with `docker build`/`docker push` requires a live Docker daemon, forcing mounting of the host's `/var/run/docker.sock` (or running directly on the host VM), which grants the job control over the node's Docker daemon equivalent to privileged access — a malicious or compromised job could use this to escape to the host.

Fix architecture: move the build onto Kubernetes via the Jenkins Kubernetes plugin — JCasC declares a kubernetes cloud with a `kaniko-builder` podTemplate, and any build labeled `kaniko` makes the plugin call the Kubernetes API to spawn a single ephemeral agent pod per build.

Pod composition: the spawned pod contains a `jnlp` container that dials back to the controller and a `kaniko` container (image `gcr.io/kaniko-project/executor`) mounting the registry secret at `/kaniko/.docker`.

Kaniko reads the Dockerfile and builds the image entirely in the pod's userspace, needing no Docker daemon and no privileged mode — only registry credentials to push — which removes the privileged-access requirement from Problem 2.

Pod lifecycle: each build pod is ephemeral — it lives for exactly one build then is destroyed (visible as `Terminating`) — so an idle system with no builds running costs zero standing background resources (no always-on VM, no idle executors).

Concurrency cap resolves Problem 1: a `containerCapStr` limit on the podTemplate (e.g., 10) caps how many build pods run in parallel, so 20 simultaneous builds are processed in capped batches instead of queuing behind one fixed-executor VM.

Verification: `kubectl -n cicd get pods -w` shows pods named `kaniko-builder-<random>` transitioning Pending → Running → Terminating per build, and the kaniko container's log reports a successful build/push with no `dockerd` process ever present in the pod.

Credentials are created at GLOBAL scope, meaning any job/team on the controller (including Growth) can read any other team's credential — this is the direct mechanism behind Growth's Jenkinsfile reading Payments' production deploy credential.

The controller keeps numExecutors > 0 to serve "urgent builds", letting builds run directly on the controller and read JENKINS_HOME plus other system secrets — expanding the attack surface well beyond a single credential.
JCasC is edited by hand via kubectl exec directly on the Pod whenever a plugin needs adding, with no PR review and no audit trail for the change.

Because the manual edit is never committed to git, the running JCasC drifts from the JCasC in git and can be silently overwritten on the next restart/reload, leaving nobody sure what config is actually live.

Proposed fix: create a dedicated jenkins_folder per team via Terraform and scope every credential (including Payments') to that team's folder rather than global, so other teams can never see it even on the same controller.
Proposed fix: enable Role-based/Matrix security so each team only has build/configure rights on its own folder and none on other teams' folders.

Proposed fix: set numExecutors: 0 on the controller and require every build to run on ephemeral Kubernetes agents (Kubernetes plugin + podTemplate), optionally further isolated by namespace/label per team.

Proposed fix: manage all JCasC (plugin config, security realm, RBAC) in git and apply it via Terraform helm_release/values, banning hand edits via kubectl exec so every change goes through a PR with plan reviewed first.

Build stage passes the artifact to the test branches via `stash`/`unstash` rather than a temp file or `archiveArtifacts`, because the artifact only needs to live for this one build run — it self-cleans when the build ends, unlike archive's long-term storage cost.
Test stage runs `Unit` and `Lint` inside a `parallel` block so they execute concurrently on separate executors, making total time ≈ max(Unit, Lint) instead of their sum.
Because parallel branches run in separate workspaces, each branch (`Unit`, `Lint`) must call `unstash 'build-output'` independently — stashed data is not automatically shared across parallel stages.

Deploy stage is gated with `when { branch 'main' }`, which is only reliable because the job is a Multibranch Pipeline: Jenkins auto-populates `env.BRANCH_NAME` for each discovered branch, whereas a single/non-multibranch job would make this gate unsafe (silent-skip risk).
The registry credential is injected via `withCredentials` with a `credentialsId` pointing into the Jenkins credential store, never hardcoded as a literal in the Jenkinsfile.

Jenkins automatically masks the bound credential variables (e.g. `$REG_USER`/`$REG_PASS`) in the console log, and the script avoids ever writing them to a file — preventing leakage via console output or a build artifact.

`post { always { cleanWs() } }` is declared at the `pipeline` level, not inside an individual stage, guaranteeing the workspace is cleaned regardless of whether `Build`, `Test`, or `Deploy` succeeds or fails.

Disagrees with the framing — what's described (CI running kubectl apply after tests pass) is push-based: CI holds the cluster's kubeconfig/credentials and actively pushes config out from outside the cluster.
GitOps inverts this push model via 4 CNCF-standardized principles.
Declarative: the whole system is described by a declarative desired state, not a sequential script.
Versioned and immutable: the desired state lives in git; every change is an auditable, revertible commit.
Pulled automatically: an agent running inside the cluster (e.g. ArgoCD's application-controller) pulls the desired state from git itself — nobody pushes from outside.
Continuously reconciled: the agent constantly compares actual state to desired state and self-heals drift, rather than a one-and-done action.

Credentials difference: push-based CI must hold kubeconfig and network access to every cluster's apiserver (expanding the attack surface across many clusters), whereas a pull-based agent only needs read access to git, so no cluster credential ever leaves that cluster.

Drift difference: push-based CI treats a one-time kubectl apply as job-done once it succeeds, with no mechanism to detect someone kubectl edit-ing by hand afterward — whereas a GitOps agent reconciles continuously, detecting and (if selfHeal is on) self-healing that drift almost immediately.

Disagrees with "Synced means it's fine": Synced only means the live state on the cluster matches the desired state in git at the current commit — it says nothing about whether the resource is actually healthy.

ArgoCD tracks health status as a separate axis from sync status, with values Healthy/Progressing/Degraded/Suspended/Missing, computed per resource kind (e.g. a Deployment is Healthy when enough replicas are ready).
The sync axis and the health axis are independent of each other — an app can be Synced (matches git) while still being Degraded.

Concrete example: git correctly declares a Deployment with a new image tag, but that image is broken so the Pod keeps crash-looping — ArgoCD applied exactly what git says (so Synced) but the Pod can't run (so Degraded).
This is exactly the scenario that matches the recurring 500 errors: checkout-service is very likely Synced + Degraded.
Before concluding the bug is "somewhere else," open the app's health tab in the ArgoCD UI (or run `argocd app get checkout-service`) to see the actual health status.
If the health status is Degraded, drill into which specific resource/Pod is unhealthy before pushing the investigation to the application layer.
Xác định nguyên nhân gốc là xung đột giữa hai controller (ArgoCD selfHeal và HPA) tranh giành cùng một field, KHÔNG phải do con người sửa tay (human drift).
Giải thích đúng cơ chế selfHeal: nó revert BẤT KỲ sai khác nào giữa live state và git desired state, bất kể sai khác đó do ai/cái gì gây ra — không chỉ kích hoạt khi có commit git mới.
Mô tả đúng thiết lập gây xung đột: manifest git hardcode `spec.replicas: 3`, trong khi HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) đang chủ động điều chỉnh replicas theo tải thực tế.

Mô tả đúng vòng lặp cụ thể: HPA tăng replicas lên (vd 8) → selfHeal thấy lệch với git nên revert về 3 → tải cao khiến HPA tăng lại → lặp vô hạn, chính là hiện tượng replica count nhảy lên-xuống liên tục mà SRE quan sát được.
Khẳng định KHÔNG nên tắt selfHeal cho toàn app, vì sẽ mất khả năng phát hiện drift thật do con người sửa tay trên các field khác.
Đề xuất phương án 1: bỏ hẳn field `replicas` khỏi manifest git, để HPA toàn quyền sở hữu field này (git không còn 'ý kiến' về replicas nên không có gì để selfHeal revert).

Đề xuất phương án 2: giữ `replicas` trong git làm giá trị baseline nhưng thêm `ignoreDifferences` cho path `/spec/replicas` trong cấu hình Application để loại trừ field này khỏi tính diff, và nhận định đây là lựa chọn an toàn/ưu tiên hơn vì vẫn giữ được giá trị mặc định rõ ràng trong git cho trường hợp HPA chưa scale.
Don't treat the whole app as generically broken — approach is to systematically find the exact stuck resource rather than guess.

Run `argocd app get orders-platform` (or the UI) to check each resource's state broken down by sync-wave, understanding that ArgoCD only advances to the next wave once ALL resources in the current wave are Healthy.

With resources at waves -1/0/1, narrow the candidates: the Namespace (wave -1) is almost certainly done quickly so it's not the culprit — the real suspects are the migration Job (wave 0) or the Deployment (wave 1).

Check the migration Job first since it blocks earlier in the chain: `kubectl -n orders describe job <migration-job>` for events — an ImagePullBackOff or a DB connection-refused error in logs would explain why the Job never completes, preventing ArgoCD from ever advancing to wave 1.

If the Job completed normally, move on to check the Deployment at wave 1: `kubectl -n orders describe pod <deployment-pod>` for FailedScheduling (insufficient resources) or a repeatedly failing readiness probe (misconfigured new image) — either explains why it stays Progressing forever.
Once the actual bottleneck resource is identified, fix the root cause — fix the Job or roll back the image — rather than guessing at the whole app.
Set a reasonable `--sync-timeout` instead of letting syncs hang indefinitely, so a future stuck resource fails fast rather than blocking forever.
Consider splitting failure-prone resources into their own sync-wave so one broken piece doesn't drag down the whole chain.

prune: true on the root Application in an app-of-apps setup doesn't just clean up child Applications no longer present in the apps/ folder — it makes ArgoCD delete EVERY resource that a child app manages.

If a child app's manifest file disappears from git (e.g. via a misplaced file deletion or a bad git revert), the next sync will prune that child app entirely, taking down the PostgreSQL StatefulSet and its PVC along with it.
This represents a disproportionate blast radius: the triggering cause is just a missing YAML file, but the consequence can be permanent production data loss if there's no separate backup.

The fix is to add the annotation argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Prune=false directly on the StatefulSet (and/or PVC) resource in the PostgreSQL child app's manifest, which excludes exactly those resources from prune behavior.
This targeted annotation lets the root Application keep prune: true for other, stateless child apps where automatic pruning is genuinely useful, rather than disabling pruning globally.
Before merging, propose testing this behavior in staging by deliberately deleting a test child app in git, running a sync, and confirming exactly what gets deleted.
Overall verdict: the manifest isn't syntactically wrong, but it overlooks a serious risk, so prune: true shouldn't be trusted on production just because it looks correct on paper.

Root cause 1 — the Prometheus query has no label filter distinguishing canary from stable (e.g. `rollouts-pod-template-hash`), so `error-rate` measures MIXED traffic from both; a spike on stable alone can push the combined ratio over threshold.
Root cause 2 — `failureLimit: 0` is overly sensitive: a single 30-second reading exceeding the 5% threshold aborts immediately, with no buffer for one isolated/transient spike.

Root cause 3 — there is no `initialDelay`, so analysis starts scoring right at the canary Pod's cold-start warm-up phase (higher latency/error from cache/JIT warm-up), and that warm-up gets mistaken for a real failure.
Fix 1 — add a label filter to both numerator and denominator of the query (e.g. `rollouts_pod_template_hash="<canary-hash>"`) so the metric measures ONLY the canary and never mixes in stable traffic.
Fix 2 — change `failureLimit` from 0 to 2 (or similar) so it takes several consecutive threshold breaches to abort, tolerating one isolated spike.
Fix 3 — add an `initialDelay` (e.g. 30s) to skip the warm-up phase before scoring begins.
Fix 4 — widen the measurement window from `[1m]` to `[5m]` to smooth out instantaneous noise.

Verification plan — re-run the canary several times with a stable build to confirm there are no more random aborts, and separately deploy a build with a genuine elevated error rate to confirm the `AnalysisRun` still aborts correctly, proving the change reduces false positives without blinding real-failure detection.
Diagnose problem 1: hand-creating N `Application` files per cluster doesn't scale, is error-prone (copy-paste), and follows no clear versionable pattern.
Propose replacing manual Applications with `ApplicationSet` using a cluster generator that automatically enumerates every cluster registered with the hub.

Describe the cluster-registration mechanism: each remote cluster is a `Secret` labeled `argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: cluster` in the hub's `argocd` namespace, holding the server URL and a ServiceAccount token.
State that the generator renders one `Application` per cluster × team combination from a single template.

Explain the payoff: adding the 4th cluster only requires registering it with the hub (`argocd cluster add`) — the cluster generator automatically produces the new Applications, with no manual file edits.
Diagnose problem 2: plaintext secrets sitting outside git violate the single-source-of-truth principle and risk exposure from manual copies across machines.

Compare sealed-secrets (private key stays only inside each cluster, `kubeseal` produces git-safe ciphertext, but that ciphertext is bound to one cluster so it must be re-sealed separately per cluster) against SOPS (client-side encryption with age/KMS produces ciphertext portable across every cluster — encrypt once, use everywhere, as long as the rendering location holds the decryption key).

Give a reasoned recommendation of SOPS for this multi-cluster, multi-region, still-growing company — portability matters more than per-cluster key isolation — and note that adopting a centralized secret manager (Vault/AWS Secrets Manager) later would justify moving to External Secrets Operator so ciphertext never needs to be committed to git at all.
